reading.body:
Obsidian is building integrations that let AI assistants directly access local note vaults rather than uploading data to cloud servers, treating the knowledge management layer as a compute attachment point rather than a data transit hub.

The two model context protocol servers listed both solve the same problem: routing AI queries into Obsidian vaults without requiring notes to leave the user's machine. One searches by title and keyword, the other connects GitHub-hosted vaults. This pattern reflects a narrowing constraint. As AI workloads grow, the bottleneck is not whether assistants can access information, but whether they can access it without the latency and privacy cost of cloud round trips. Local-first architecture compresses that path.

For AI scaling specifically, this matters because inference is increasingly bottlenecked by context retrieval and data freshness rather than model capability. If a system must ping a cloud database for every query, response time degrades and power consumption multiplies. Routing inference directly to local storage layers reduces both. Obsidian's approach assumes users will keep their knowledge stores on edge devices, not cloud vaults, which trades off centralized compute for distributed inference efficiency.

The data does not reveal whether these integrations materially change how much compute Obsidian itself requires to maintain, or whether they reduce network traffic at scale. It shows surface integration points but not adoption or the actual queries these servers handle.

profile_text.body:
Obsidian is a for-profit startup founded in 2020 and headquartered in Los Angeles, California. It publishes a note-taking application that its site describes as a free and flexible app for private thoughts. According to the company, notes are stored privately on the user's own device and remain accessible offline, and no one else can read them, not even the company. The site lists uses including personal notes, journaling, knowledge bases, and project management, along with linked notes, a visual graph of relationships between notes, a space called Canvas for research and diagramming, and thousands of plugins supported by an open API.

Its tracked AI product is Obsidian AI, described as a local-first knowledge AI that is privacy-focused, works through plugins, and has no cloud dependency. Two MCP servers are listed for it: one that connects AI assistants to a GitHub-hosted Obsidian vault for access, search, and analysis, and one that searches a vault to find notes by title or keyword and summarize related content.

The record also lists a California law exposure count of 270, with no individual cases named.
